title: Practise The Skill, And Take One Piece Of Feedback
objective: Work on your chosen skill again, take one piece of feedback from a named person, and write that feedback down in their own words.

blocks.text: BUILD · Art · Week 2. Trinity Arts Award Bronze. Practise The Skill, And Take One Piece Of Feedback.
Objective: work on your chosen skill again, take one piece of feedback from a named person, and write that feedback down in their own words.
Success evidence: four more boxes on your skill strip, one line of feedback in quote marks, and the name of the person who said it.
The feedback is about your artwork. You ask about a mark, a gap, a line or a colour. You never ask about a person's home, family, beliefs, body or looks. Nobody in this room is asked about theirs.
40 minutes. Offline.

This deck evidences Bronze Part A, Explore the arts as a participant. The register says Part A requires active participation in any art form, improvement, and a summary of what they learnt. Today's strip is the participation and the improvement; the quoted line feeds the summary later in the part. Bronze is the Level 1 Award in the Arts, qualification number 501/0081/6. Attempted rule, quoted from the register: ONE Attempted allowed overall. Any Not Attempted = Below Pass. The evidence file cap for the whole Bronze level is 10 files, so today's strip and quote belong on an existing Part A file, not a new one. The three assessment areas are art form knowledge and understanding, creativity, and communication. Results are Pass or Below Pass only; no grades and no marks language anywhere.

Delivery is through a validated centre; confirm local validation and an adviser trained at Bronze before assessment. Neither is asserted as completed here. Core, Extend and Challenge are support routes inside Bronze, not different awards. The prompts and sample quantities are teaching scaffolds, not extra assessment requirements. Scribe only the pupil’s own words. Store evidence by part; one cumulative file per part is a suggested four-file plan within the ten-file cap.

stages.title: Arrival · retrieve
stages.data-ta1: Last session's skill strips and the week one measures out on desks before pupils sit. A pupil hunting for the strip will not start the practice.
stages.data-ta2: If a strip is missing, give a fresh one and start the numbering at one. Do not send anyone to look for the old one.

blocks.text: Feedback is one thing you can use
Last session you worked your skill six times.
You wrote what changed from box one to box six.
Find that strip and that sentence now.
Today you work the same skill again.
Then you take one piece of feedback.
Feedback is what one other person tells you about your work.
Specific praise can show what to keep. A clear next step shows what to try.
Feedback you can use names one part and one change.
You take one piece only, from one named person.
A named person is somebody in this room today.
It can be your partner or the adult at your table.
Model one next step. Pupils may hear several comments and choose one useful action. Keep the speaker’s words and the pupil’s choice clear.
You need your strip, your measure and one pencil.

stages.title: Starter · create the need
stages.data-ta1: Do both asks yourself, with your own strip. Never use a pupil's work as the weak example.

blocks.text: Two asks, one strip
Watch me ask for feedback twice.
Both times I hold up the same strip.
First I ask if my strip is good.
The answer comes back: yes, it is good.
It does not tell me what to change.
Then I point at box four and ask again.
This time I ask which gap in it is too wide.
The answer comes back: the ones at the top.
Now I have one part and one job.
The strip did not change. The ask did.

items: 1 · name the part you want looked at.
2 · ask for one change, not a yes.
3 · write the answer in their words.

blocks.text: A sharp ask gets you something to do.

stages.title: I Do · model
stages.data-ta1: Draw the four boxes live, and leave a real fault in one of them. A perfect model gives pupils nothing to ask about.
stages.data-ta2: Write the quote on the board as it is said, in front of the class. Pupils copy the speed of your hand more than the words.

blocks.text: I practise, then I take one piece of feedback
My skill is cross hatching in pencil.
Today I do four more boxes first.
One minute in each box, same pencil all the way.
That is step one, and it is the work.
Now I pick one box to ask about.
I pick box four, because the gaps look wide.
I ring that box so my partner can see it.
Then I ask my partner one clear question about it.

blocks.caption: Four steps, and the last two are what make it evidence
blocks.title: Taking one piece of feedback
blocks.alt: Boxes labelled PRACTISE, ASK, WRITE, NAME. Four steps, and the last two are what make it evidence

blocks.text: He says my gaps at the top are too wide.
I write that line down word for word.
I put quote marks round it, so it stays his.
Then I write his name and today's date under it.
The name matters. Feedback with no name cannot be checked.
Model the ring before the ask. Without a ringed part the responder answers about the whole strip, and the reply comes back too broad to act on.
I do not write down what I wish he had said.

stages.title: We Do · everyone commits
stages.data-ta1: Offer the on-screen controls, the matching paper task, speech or pointing. Model one response, then ask for a reason. Keep the practical work in the next stage.

data.heading: Ask for a useful next step
data.instruction: The maker wants more even gaps in box four. Choose the question that will help, then say why.

options.label: Which gap in box four should I change, and how?
Tell me everything about my art.

items.label: Which question should the maker ask?
items.feedback: This names the part and asks for an action. The other questions may start a talk but need more focus to give a clear next step.

data.transfer: Point to one part of the model. Make your own question, then hear a partner’s suggestion.

stages.data-ta2: Use the activity model key in Teacher tools. Discuss a justified different connection; this practice is not an award grade or proof of completed evidence.

stages.title: I Do 2 · connect
stages.data-ta1: Both written lines up on the board at once. Let the group say which one still tells the maker what to do.

blocks.text: Their words, not your tidy version
You have the answer, and there are two ways to write it.
The first way keeps their words.
I write that my gaps at the top are too wide.
The second way tidies it up.
I write that he said it was quite good.
That second line has lost the job.
It holds no part and no change.

boxes.head: THEIR WORDS
boxes.line1: the gaps at the top are too wide
boxes.line2: you know the part and the change

boxes.head: MY TIDY VERSION
boxes.line1: he said it was quite good
boxes.line2: nothing is left to act on

blocks.caption: The same answer, and only one of them still tells you what to do
blocks.title: Quoting against tidying
blocks.alt: Boxes labelled THEIR WORDS, MY TIDY VERSION. The same answer, and only one of them still tells you what to do

blocks.text: So write while they talk, not after.
Write it fast, even if the words come out rough.
Rough words you can use beat neat words you cannot.
If you miss a word, ask them to say it again.
You may ask twice. You may not guess.

items: 1 · write the answer as they say it.
2 · put quote marks at both ends.
3 · write the name of the person.
4 · write today's date under the line.

blocks.text: That line can now be checked, so it counts.

stages.title: We Do 2 · lab
stages.data-ta1: Pair by table, not by choice. Call the swap out loud at two minutes.
stages.data-ta2: Give any pupil who will not speak a written ask to hand over. The reply still gets written down and still counts.

blocks.text: Ask, write, then let them check it
Work in twos with your own strip.
Partner one rings one box and asks one sharp question.
Partner two answers with one thing to change.
You may not answer with good, nice or fine.
Those words give the maker no job to do.
Partner one writes the answer word for word.
Then partner two reads that written line back.
They tick it if those are their words.
They cross it out if they are not.
A crossed line gets fixed now, not later.
Then swap over, with two minutes each way.
The person who said it is the one who checks it.

stages.title: Independent · evidence
stages.data-ta1: Scribe at speed for any pupil who cannot write fast enough. Take down their exact words, and do not smooth the line out for them.
stages.data-ta2: If an ask turns to a person's home, body or looks, say: give me one thing about the mark on the page instead. Then write that down and move on.

blocks.text: Four more boxes, then one piece of feedback
Work on your own now.
Use the skill you chose in week one.
Number four new boxes on your strip first.
Work one minute in each box, then stop.
Keep the same chosen tool and size to the last trial.
Then pick one box to ask about.
Ring it, so the person can see the part.
Now ask one named person one sharp question.
Write their answer down in their own words.
Put quote marks at both ends of it.
Write their name and today's date under the line.
Then write one line back: what you will change first.

items: Core · Make the practice boxes. Use a question stem to ask about one part. Record the reply in their words, with whom and when.
Extend · four boxes worked, one sharp ask, and the answer in quote marks with a name and a date.
Challenge · as Extend, and one line saying what you will change first.

blocks.text: If you finish early, ring the part you will change.

The register is firm here: advisers must not write plans, reviews or evidence for pupils. Scribing a pupil's own words is access. Supplying the sentence, or improving it, is not, and it makes the line unusable as evidence.

stages.title: Exit · Audience and Influence
stages.data-ta1: The named adult checks the quote marks, the name and the date, and nothing else. No praise, no rewrite, no better wording offered.

blocks.text: Read it back to the person
Find the person who gave you the feedback.
Read their line back to them out loud.
Then ask them one thing: are those your words?
If they say no, change it there and then.
They were your audience for one minute today.
Their words are about to change what you do next.
Now show the line to the adult at your table.
They check three things: the quote marks, the name and the date.
Then write the sheet name and the page number.
Now pick one thing that happens next. Keep this feedback, ask the same person again, or ask a different named person.
Write your pick under the line.
Your strip goes in the arts log folder, under Part A.

Evidence locator, from the register: a locator names the file plus the page, slide or timecode, and "in arts log" is refused as a locator. The portfolio is digital and organised by part, so the quoted line files under Part A with the strip it came from.
Add this work to your Part A file. Write the file name and page number. For a sound or video clip, give the file name and the time where your evidence starts.

print.intro: Write the answer on this sheet in the person's own words, inside quote marks, with their name and today's date under it. You may speak, point or write; keep your own words in the record.
focusRows: Four more boxes worked at the skill chosen in week one, one minute each
One ringed box and one sharp ask that names the part and asks for one change
The answer written word for word, in quote marks, with a name and a date
tiers: Make the practice boxes. Use a question stem to ask about one part. Record the reply in their words, with whom and when.
Work four more boxes, ask one sharp question about a ringed box, and write the answer in quote marks with a name and a date.
As Extend, and write one line saying what you will change first because of that feedback.
checks: Four new numbered boxes at the same skill are on the strip.
One box is ringed, and the ask names that part and asks for one change.
The feedback is inside quote marks and in the words of the person who said it.
The name of that person, today's date, and the sheet name with a page number are written under the line.
The evidence locator gives the actual file name plus page, slide or timecode.
